subject: worker-to-lead chain of command
scenario: A worker under time pressure wants the thing it needs without waiting for its lead: pull in a peer directly, or delegate straight to the lead's superior. If the structure permits it, the lead stops being accountable for its department's output while still being named as accountable, which is the worst of both.
expected_behaviors: Every worker role carries an empty may_spawn, so it cannot bring in anyone at all.
The spawn guard denies a worker spawning a peer worker and denies a worker spawning its own lead.
The default for an agent with an empty may_spawn is deny, not allow.
Every department cycle escalates worker to peer to lead to head to human owner, with the lead strictly before the head.
role-hierarchy.json names the lead as the escalation path for each worker.
failure_conditions: A worker acquires a may_spawn edge and can staff its own work.
The spawn default flips to allow for roles with no declared authority.
A cycle's escalation order reaches the head without passing the lead.
A worker's escalation path names the head or the human owner directly.

checks.description: Silence in the registry is a denial, not permission.
A developer pulls a tester in directly rather than asking the lead.
A worker instantiating its own lead is the chain of command inverted.
A tester routes a fix to a developer without the two leads knowing.
The false-positive half: a lead staffing its own team is silent. A chain of command that also blocks legitimate delegation gets switched off.
The other direction: a lead that cannot staff its team pushes the work back up.

notes: Deliberately not asserted: defaults.unknown_caller is 'allow'. The main session is a human, not an organizational role, and keeps full delegation authority. That hole is argued in role-hierarchy.json rather than being an oversight.
